name: Password storage and authentication-scheme analysis
theory_paragraphs: Start from zero: a \term{cryptographic hash function} $H$ is a publicly known algorithm that takes an input of ANY length (a password, a file, a string) and produces a fixed-length output called a \term{digest} (for example 256 bits). Three properties matter for this exam topic:\begin{tightitem}\item \term{Deterministic}: the same input always gives the same digest, so the server can re-hash what you type and compare it with what it stored.\item \term{One-way} (also called \term{preimage resistant}): given a digest $y$, it is computationally infeasible to find ANY input $x$ with $H(x) = y$. The only known generic strategy is to guess candidates and hash them.\item \term{Collision resistant}: it is infeasible to find two different inputs with the same digest.\end{tightitem}Why store hashes at all? If the server kept passwords in plaintext and an attacker stole the database, every account would be compromised instantly. If instead the server stores $H(password)$, the thief only gets digests, and one-wayness forces her into \term{guessing}: pick a candidate password, hash it, compare with the stored digest. This guessing game is the whole topic.

The threat model in these problems is the \term{offline attack}: the attacker (usually called Mallory) has already stolen a copy of the password database and hashes candidates on her own machine at her own speed -- there is no server to rate-limit her and no lockout to slow her down. The reason guessing works in practice is that humans pick terrible passwords: the exam models this by saying every password comes from a publicly known list of $L$ candidates (a \term{dictionary}). Guessing all $L$ candidates against one stored digest therefore costs at most $L$ hash evaluations. A \term{rainbow table} pushes this further: an attacker precomputes the digest of every candidate ONCE, stores the (digest, password) pairs, and then cracks any unsalted digest with a pure table lookup -- zero new hashes. Exam cost model: \imp{only hash evaluations count} -- comparisons, concatenations, and database reads/writes are free.

The classic defense is a \term{salt}: a random, per-user value that is PUBLIC (stored in cleartext next to the digest). The server stores $(username,\; s,\; H(s \,\|\, password))$. Because the salt differs per user, the digest function differs per user, so one precomputed dictionary no longer fits all users -- rainbow tables die. The salt is not meant to be secret; its entire job is to destroy reuse across users. Two facts to memorize:\begin{tightitem}\item \imp{a single global salt is not a salt} -- if every user shares the same salt, all digests still share one function and rainbow tables work again.\item A \term{slow hash / KDF} (bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2, PBKDF2 -- essentially $H$ iterated tens of thousands of times) multiplies the cost of EVERY guess by a huge constant; a legitimate user logs in once and barely notices, but an attacker making billions of guesses cannot afford it.\end{tightitem}

Every cost-accounting sub-question is solved by one principle: \term{factor the stored-value formula} into two kinds of subexpressions.\begin{tightitem}\item \term{User-independent subexpressions} -- anything built only from the password, e.g. $H(password)$: precompute once for all $L$ candidates and reuse the result for every user.\item \term{Per-user subexpressions} -- anything the username or a per-user salt touches, e.g. $H(username \,\|\, password)$: must be recomputed from scratch for each of the $U$ users.\end{tightitem}The PLACEMENT of $H$ decides everything: an $H$ wrapped around the whole expression (username included) forces $U \cdot L$ fresh evaluations, while $H(password)$ sitting as an inner term can be precomputed into a dictionary costing only $L$ once. The four canonical shapes, for recovering all passwords:\begin{tightitem}\item $H(password)$: $L$ hashes (one dictionary serves all users).\item $H(username \,\|\, password)$: $U \cdot L$ hashes (no reuse possible).\item $H(H(username) \,\|\, password)$: $U + U \cdot L$ hashes (precompute $H(username)$ once per user).\item $H(username \,\|\, H(password))$: $L + U \cdot L$ hashes (precompute the $L$ hashed passwords).\end{tightitem}For the replacement attack (set every password to pwned) the same factoring applies, but remember the classic trap: \imp{pwned is not in the candidate list}, so its inner hash can never come from the precomputed dictionary -- it costs one extra evaluation.

The second scheme family is the \term{Lamport hash chain} (one-time passwords). At registration the client computes $H^{N}(pwd \,\|\, salt)$ -- apply $H$ a total of $N$ times, where $H^{0}(x) = x$ and $H^{3}(x) = H(H(H(x)))$ -- and the server stores it in a variable $stored$. At login number $i$ the client sends $H^{N-i}(pwd \,\|\, salt)$; the server checks $H(\text{received}) = stored$ and, on success, updates $stored := \text{received}$. Think of the chain as a rope with exponent marks: registration hangs the top value $H^{N}(pwd \,\|\, salt)$ on the server as $stored$, and each login uses a mark one LOWER than the last ($H^{N-i}$, then $H^{N-i-1}$, and so on). Hashing moves you UP the rope, from exponent $k$ to $k+1$, toward the registered top value -- that is exactly what the server does to verify: it hashes the received token once and compares with $stored$. One-wayness means nobody can step DOWN the rope: going from the token just sent, $H^{N-i}(pwd \,\|\, salt)$, to the next login's token, $H^{N-i-1}(pwd \,\|\, salt)$, would require inverting $H$, which is infeasible. Consequences, all of which have appeared on exams:\begin{tightitem}\item The server needs to know NEITHER $pwd$ NOR $salt$ -- it only hashes the received token once and compares; the client built the whole chain at registration.\item The next token $H^{N-i-1}(pwd \,\|\, salt)$ CANNOT be derived from the token just sent -- that would mean inverting $H$ once. The client must recompute it from $pwd \,\|\, salt$ at a cost of $N-i-1$ hash evaluations.\item At login $i = N$ the client sends $H^{0}(pwd \,\|\, salt) = pwd \,\|\, salt$ in plaintext, so a network eavesdropper learns the password exactly there.\item An attacker who can WRITE $stored$ picks any value $v$, sets $stored := H(v)$, and logs in by sending $v$ -- no knowledge of $pwd$, $salt$, or $i$ required.\end{tightitem}

Design-critique questions (the third exam family) reuse four terms you must define before you can argue with them.\begin{tightitem}\item \term{Kerckhoffs' principle}: a system's security must depend ONLY on the secrecy of the key (here: the password), never on the secrecy of the algorithm. Public algorithms are attacked by thousands of experts and survive; a secret home-grown hash often hides fatal flaws, and the moment its design leaks, everything breaks at once. So \q{our experts invented a secret hash} is a weakness, not a strength.\item \term{Denial of service (DoS)}: an attack that steals nothing but makes the system unusable for legitimate users. Example: if an account locks after 3 failed logins, an attacker can deliberately fail 3 logins on YOUR username to lock you out -- this is called user-targeted DoS.\item \term{Two-factor authentication (2FA)}: login requires two independent proofs, typically \q{something you know} (a password) plus \q{something you have} (a phone or hardware token). A stolen password alone no longer suffices, which is why 2FA is the standard fix for weak-password and password-reset problems.\item \term{Trusted computing base (TCB)}: the set of all hardware, software, and PEOPLE that must behave correctly for the system to stay secure. Every fallback server and every extra administrator enlarges the TCB, and a larger TCB means more components whose compromise breaks everything.\end{tightitem}\imp{define every term you use} in a critique answer -- the grader cannot give points for an argument built on undefined vocabulary.
theory_cheatsheet: Cost model: only hash evaluations count; comparisons, concatenation and DB operations are free.
Unsalted $H(password)$: recover all $U$ passwords costs $L$ hashes; set all to pwned costs $1$ hash.
Username/salt inside the OUTER hash kills reuse: recovery $U \cdot L$, replacement $U$.
$H(password)$ as an INNER term: precompute the dictionary once: recovery $L + U \cdot L$; replacement $1 + U$ (pwned is NOT in the list, so its inner hash costs 1 extra).
$H(username)$ as an inner term: precomputable once per user, adding a flat $+U$ term.

Lamport chain: login $i$ sends $H^{N-i}(pwd \,\|\, salt)$; server checks $H(\text{received}) = stored$; the next token cannot be derived from the current one (one-wayness); login $N$ leaks $pwd$ in plaintext; a DB-writer sets $stored := H(v)$ and logs in with $v$.
identify_givens: A password database with $U$ users whose passwords come from a known list of $L$ candidates, a concrete storage formula built from a secure hash $H$ and concatenation (e.g. $H(password)$, $H(username \,\|\, password)$, $H(H(username) \,\|\, password)$, $H(username \,\|\, H(password))$), and an attacker Mallory who can read and modify the database; or a Lamport-style hash-chain scheme using $H^{k}(pwd \,\|\, salt)$ with a server-side \q{stored} variable and a network- or server-compromising attacker; or a list of organizational password measures to critique. Only hash computations count as cost; comparisons and database operations are free.
identify_target: For each storage scheme, describe the attack and compute the exact number of hash evaluations needed (a) to recover every user's password and (b) to change every password to a fixed new value such as \q{pwned}; or, for hash-chain schemes, justify what the server must know, compute the chain index/cost of the next login, state at which login an eavesdropper learns the password, and show how a server-compromising attacker logs in without $pwd$, $salt$, or the login index; or, for design critiques, map each measure to the threats it counters, the vulnerabilities it leaves or introduces, and better countermeasures.

algorithm.detail: Write down the exact stored-value formula, the attacker's capabilities (read DB, modify DB, eavesdrop logins, compromise server), and the goal:\begin{tightitem}\item \term{recovery}: determine every user's password;\item \term{replacement}: overwrite all entries so every password becomes a fixed new value (e.g. pwned).\end{tightitem}Recall the cost model: \imp{only hash evaluations count}.

Split the hash expression into\begin{tightitem}\item \term{user-independent subexpressions} -- precompute once, reuse for all users. E.g. $H(password)$ is the same for every user: a dictionary of all $L$ values costs $L$ hashes total.\item \term{per-user subexpressions} -- anything concatenated with the username or a per-user salt must be recomputed for each user.\end{tightitem}This factoring decides the entire answer.

For each of the $U$ users, test all $L$ candidates against the stored value; total = (one-time precomputation) $+\; U \times L \times$ (hashes per candidate after reuse). The four canonical shapes:\begin{tightitem}\item $H(pwd)$: $L$ (one dictionary serves all users).\item $H(user \,\|\, pwd)$: $U \cdot L$ (salt kills reuse).\item $H(H(user) \,\|\, pwd)$: $U + U \cdot L$ (precompute $H(user)$ per user).\item $H(user \,\|\, H(pwd))$: $L + U \cdot L$ (precompute the $L$ hashed passwords).\end{tightitem}

Apply the same factoring to the new password pwned: compute its user-independent inner hash once if the formula needs it, then one outer hash per user:\begin{tightitem}\item $H(pwned)$: $1$ hash, written everywhere.\item $H(user \,\|\, pwned)$: $U$ hashes.\item $H(H(user) \,\|\, pwned)$: $U + U = 2U$.\item $H(user \,\|\, H(pwned))$: $1 + U$.\end{tightitem}Trap: \imp{pwned is not in the candidate list}, so its inner hash can never come from the dictionary precomputation -- it costs one extra evaluation.

If a goal requires inverting $H$ (recovering a password outside the candidate list, or walking a hash chain backwards), state that it is \term{infeasible because $H$ is one-way}. Likewise state that the server only needs to know the values it actually compares -- it never needs $pwd$ or $salt$ themselves.

For Lamport-style schemes where login $i$ sends $H^{N-i}(pwd \,\|\, salt)$ and the server checks $H(\text{received}) = stored$ then updates $stored$:\begin{tightitem}\item The next login needs exponent $N-i-1$; it CANNOT be derived from the sent value (one-wayness) and costs full recomputation from $pwd \,\|\, salt$, i.e. $N-i-1$ hashes.\item At login $N$ the client sends $H^{0}(pwd \,\|\, salt) = pwd \,\|\, salt$ in plaintext -- an eavesdropper learns the password here.\item An attacker who can write $stored$ sets $stored := H(v)$ for a chosen $v$ and logs in with $v$ -- no knowledge of $pwd$, $salt$, or $i$ required.\end{tightitem}

Give the final count per scheme and per goal as a closed formula in $U$ and $L$ (e.g. $L$ and $1$; $U \cdot L$ and $U$; $U + U \cdot L$ and $2U$; $L + U \cdot L$ and $U + 1$), each with one line of justification naming what was precomputed and what is per-user.

For design-critique questions, process the listed measures ONE AT A TIME, and for each measure answer the four required axes in order:\begin{tightitem}\item \term{Threats countered}: name the concrete attack the measure defends against (e.g. hashing protects the stolen file; a salt counters rainbow tables; composition rules counter dictionary attacks; lockout counters ONLINE guessing).\item \term{Remaining vulnerabilities}: state what still breaks. Recurring findings: a single global salt is not a salt (rainbow tables still work); a secret proprietary hash violates \term{Kerckhoffs' principle}; extra servers/admins enlarge the \term{trusted computing base}; harsh rules push users to write passwords down; lockout enables user-targeted \term{denial of service}; a reset channel with no authentication lets anyone take over an account.\item \term{Better countermeasure}: per-user salts with a public, well-studied, ideally slow KDF (bcrypt/scrypt/Argon2/PBKDF2); server hardening and least privilege; turn strict rules into recommendations plus breached-password checks and \term{two-factor authentication}; e-mail reset links and backoff/captcha instead of hard lockout.\item \term{Decision factors}: cost versus benefit, the security level the service actually needs, usability (onerous rules backfire), and the overall security state of the company.\end{tightitem}Use the defined terms explicitly -- \imp{define every term you use}.

variations.name: Hash placement / nesting
variations.detail: The professor permutes where $H$ and the username sit: $H(password)$, $H(username \,\|\, password)$, $H(H(username) \,\|\, password)$, $H(username \,\|\, H(password))$. Where the inner hash sits decides what is reusable: a dictionary of $H(pwd)$ is reusable across users only when $H(pwd)$ appears as an INNER term (giving $L + U \cdot L$ instead of $U \cdot L$); $H(username)$ is precomputable once per user (adding a flat $U$). Trap: forgetting that pwned is not in the $L$-list, so its inner hash costs one extra evaluation in the replacement attack ($U + 1$, not $U$).

variations.name: Lamport hash-chain login
variations.detail: Instead of a static database, the scheme sends $H^{N-i}(pwd \,\|\, salt)$ at login $i$ and the server verifies $H(\text{received}) = stored$. Sub-questions ask whether the server needs $pwd$/$salt$ (no -- it only compares hashes), the cost of the next login (full recomputation; the chain cannot be walked backwards), when an eavesdropper learns $pwd$ (at $i = N$, since $H^{0}(x) = x$ is sent in plaintext), and the server-compromise attack (set $stored := H(v)$, log in with $v$). Trap: thinking the next token can be derived from the current one -- one-wayness forbids it.

variations.name: Role reversal: attacker writes the database
variations.detail: The second goal always flips the attacker from reader to writer: instead of cracking, Mallory replaces stored hashes so every user has password pwned. The cost structure mirrors recovery but with $L$ replaced by the single value pwned. Traps: reusing the dictionary of $L$ password hashes for pwned (impossible -- pwned is not in the list), or forgetting that the per-user salt forces $U$ separate outer hashes.

variations.name: Design-critique checklist
variations.detail: Other sittings list organizational measures (secret proprietary hash, one global \q{salt}, strict composition rules, forced rotation, lockout, phone recovery) and ask which attack each counters. Map each measure: a proprietary hash violates \term{Kerckhoffs' principle}; a global salt is not a salt and does not stop rainbow tables -- only per-user salts do; lockout/rate limiting stops ONLINE guessing but enables user-targeted DoS; a \term{slow KDF} (bcrypt/scrypt/Argon2/PBKDF2) raises OFFLINE cracking cost. Adapt by naming the attack each measure does and does not address.

walkthrough_steps.work: First write down what is being asked before touching any formula. Goal (1) is \term{recovery}: Trudy wants every user's actual password. Goal (2) is \term{replacement}: she wants to overwrite the database so every password becomes letmein. The cost model says \imp{only hash evaluations count} -- so when we count, we ignore comparisons and database writes entirely. Beginner mistake to avoid: do not count the $U \times L$ comparisons; only the hashes. For the prototype login, Trudy additionally eavesdrops the network (part iii) and can write $stored$ (part iv).

Now do the factoring step -- this decides everything, so spend your time here. In (a) the whole stored value is $H(password)$: no username anywhere, so it is fully \term{user-independent}. In (b) and (d) the username is concatenated with the password INSIDE the outer hash, so nothing about the password can be reused across users. In (c) the inner term $H(password)$ is user-independent (one dictionary of $L$ values works for everyone) but the OUTER hash mixes in the username, forcing per-user work. In (d) the inner $H(username)$ is constant per user, so it is precomputable once per user. Why this matters: every candidate you test against user 1's digest in scheme (b) is useless for user 2, because the username changed the input to $H$. For the replacement attack, note the trap now: letmein is not in the candidate list, so $H(letmein)$ can never come from the precomputed dictionary -- it costs one fresh hash wherever an inner $H(pwd)$ is needed.

(a) Compute $H(candidate)$ for each of the $L$ candidates once, then compare this dictionary against all $U$ stored digests: \[ L \text{ hashes.} \] The comparisons are free, so the $U$ digests cost nothing extra. (b) The username sits inside the outer hash, so the dictionary idea fails: for EACH user, hash all $L$ candidates concatenated with that user's name, giving \[ U \cdot L \text{ hashes.} \] (c) Precompute the dictionary $H(candidate)$ for all $L$ candidates ($L$ hashes, reused for every user), then per user compute the outer hash $H(H(candidate) \,\|\, username)$ for all $L$ candidates ($U \cdot L$ hashes): \[ L + U \cdot L \text{ hashes.} \] (d) Precompute $H(username)$ once per user ($U$ hashes total), then per user compute $H(candidate \,\|\, H(username))$ for all $L$ candidates ($U \cdot L$ hashes): \[ U + U \cdot L \text{ hashes.} \] Sanity check for beginners: the total is always (one-time precomputation) plus $U \cdot L$ times the per-candidate work that remains after reuse.

Now Trudy flips from reader to writer; the factoring from Step 2 still applies. (a) Compute $H(letmein)$ once and write it into all $U$ entries: $1$ hash (writes are free). (b) Per user compute $H(letmein \,\|\, username)$: $U$ hashes. (c) Compute $H(letmein)$ once -- \imp{letmein is not in the candidate list}, so the dictionary from Step 3 does NOT contain it -- then per user compute $H(H(letmein) \,\|\, username)$: \[ 1 + U \text{ hashes.} \] (d) Per user compute $H(username)$ ($U$ hashes, counted fresh here; if you already did the recovery phase you may note the reuse) and per user compute $H(letmein \,\|\, H(username))$ ($U$ hashes): \[ 2U \text{ hashes.} \] Common beginner error: writing $U$ for (c) by assuming the dictionary covers letmein -- it does not, because letmein is not among the $L$ candidates.

Part (i): the server needs NEITHER $pwd$ NOR $salt$. Look at what the server actually does: it computes ONE hash of the received token and compares it with $stored$. The chain was created by the client at registration; the server only ever sees digests. This is the standard exam justification: name the exact operations the server performs (one hash, one comparison, one update) and observe that $pwd$ and $salt$ appear in none of them. Part (ii), first half: deriving the next token $H^{499-i}(pwd \,\|\, salt)$ from the token $H^{500-i}(pwd \,\|\, salt)$ just sent would require inverting $H$ exactly once, which is infeasible because $H$ is \term{one-way}. Whenever a question asks \q{can X be derived from Y}, check whether it requires reversing a hash -- if yes, the answer is no, citing one-wayness.

Part (ii), second half: at login $i+1$ the client must send $H^{500-(i+1)}(pwd \,\|\, salt) = H^{499-i}(pwd \,\|\, salt)$. Since it cannot be derived from the previous token, the client recomputes it from $pwd \,\|\, salt$ by applying $H$ exactly $499 - i$ times, costing \[ 499 - i \text{ hash evaluations.} \] Part (iii): at login $i = 500$ the client sends $H^{0}(pwd \,\|\, salt)$, and by definition $H^{0}(x) = x$, so the wire literally carries $pwd \,\|\, salt$ in plaintext. An eavesdropper therefore learns the password at the 500th login (and at no earlier login, because all earlier tokens are digests and $H$ is one-way). Part (iv): Trudy picks ANY value $v$ of her choice, overwrites $stored := H(v)$, and sends $v$ as her login token. The server computes $H(v)$, finds it equal to $stored$, accepts, and updates $stored := v$. She never needed $pwd$, $salt$, or $i$ -- the server-side check only compares one hash, so whoever controls $stored$ controls login.

Collect the answers as closed formulas with one-line justifications. (a) recovery $L$, replacement $1$ (fully user-independent); (b) recovery $U \cdot L$, replacement $U$ (username inside the outer hash kills all reuse); (c) recovery $L + U \cdot L$, replacement $U + 1$ (dictionary of $H(candidate)$ reused; letmein costs one extra hash); (d) recovery $U + U \cdot L$, replacement $2U$ ($H(username)$ precomputed once per user). Prototype login: the server needs neither $pwd$ nor $salt$; login $i+1$ requires a fresh $H^{499-i}(pwd \,\|\, salt)$ costing $499 - i$ hashes; $pwd \,\|\, salt$ leaks in plaintext at login $500$; a DB-writing attacker logs in by setting $stored := H(v)$ and sending $v$.

exam_questions.source: Regular exam (exam-with-solutions.pdf), Problem 2: Authentication -- Password Storage [12 points]
exam_questions.problem:
Alice maintains a database of passwords with $U$ users. Each user has a unique username and chooses a (not necessarily unique) password from a list of $L$ passwords; $U$ and $L$ are positive integers, and $H$ is a secure cryptographic hash function. Mallory can read and modify (read, add, update, delete) Alice's database and wants to achieve two goals: (1) compute the password of every user; (2) change the password of every user to \q{pwned}, a password that is NOT in the list of $L$ passwords. For each storage scheme below, describe the two attacks and determine how many hashes Mallory needs to compute for each (otherwise justify why it is not possible). Only hash computations count; comparisons and database reads/modifications are free.
\begin{tightitem}
\item[(a)] [3p] store: username and $H(password)$.
\item[(b)] [3p] store: username and $H(username ++ password)$, where $++$ denotes string concatenation.
\item[(c)] [3p] store: username and $H(H(username) ++ password)$.
\item[(d)] [3p] store: username and $H(username ++ H(password))$.
\end{tightitem}

solution_steps.work: Two goals: recovery (find all $U$ passwords) and replacement (set every password to pwned). Cost model: only hash evaluations count -- the comparisons against the database and the writes back are free. Mallory may read and modify the database, so both attacks are available to her.

(a) $H(password)$ is fully user-independent: one dictionary of all $L$ candidate hashes is reusable for every user. (b) the username is inside the (only) hash, so nothing is reusable -- the username acts as a per-user salt. (c) the inner term $H(username)$ is constant per user and precomputable once per user; the outer hash still mixes in that per-user value, so the password part needs $U \cdot L$ work. (d) the inner term $H(password)$ is user-independent (dictionary of $L$ reusable), but the outer hash concatenates the username, forcing per-user work. For the replacement attack, note: pwned is not in the list of $L$ passwords, so $H(pwned)$ must be computed fresh wherever an inner password hash is needed.

(a) Mallory computes the hash of each of the $L$ possible passwords and compares with the list of hashes from the database: \[ L \text{ hashes.} \] (b) The hashes are effectively salted by the username, so Mallory must hash the entire list of $L$ passwords once for every user: \[ U \times L \text{ hashes.} \] (c) First compute the hash of each username, a list of $U$ hashed usernames ($U$ hashes); then, for each user, combine their hashed username with all $L$ passwords ($U \times L$ outer hashes): \[ U + U \times L \text{ hashes.} \] (d) First compute the hash of the entire list of $L$ possible passwords ($L$ hashes, reused for all users); then, for each username, compute the hash of the username concatenated with each of the $L$ hashed passwords ($U \times L$ outer hashes): \[ L + U \times L \text{ hashes.} \]

(a) Compute the hash of pwned once and replace every user's stored hash with it: \[ 1 \text{ hash.} \] (b) Because the hash is salted with the username, compute $H(username ++ pwned)$ separately for every user and replace the database with the matching $(username, H(username ++ pwned))$ pairs: \[ U \text{ hashes.} \] (c) First hash each username ($U$ hashes), then compute the outer hash of each hashed username concatenated with pwned (another $U$ hashes): \[ 2 \times U \text{ hashes.} \] (d) Compute $H(pwned)$ once -- pwned is not in the list, so the precomputed dictionary does not help -- then hash it together with each of the $U$ usernames: \[ U + 1 \text{ hashes.} \]

(a) $L$ and $1$; (b) $U \times L$ and $U$; (c) $U + U \times L$ and $2 \times U$; (d) $L + U \times L$ and $U + 1$. Each figure is justified by what could be precomputed once (user-independent terms) versus what had to be recomputed per user (terms the username touches).

exam_questions.answer: (a) $L$ hashes to recover, $1$ to replace; (b) $U \times L$ and $U$; (c) $U + U \times L$ and $2U$; (d) $L + U \times L$ and $U + 1$.

exam_questions.source: Regular exam (exam-problems-with-solutions.pdf), Problem 2: Authentication -- Password Storage (hash chain) [10 points]
exam_questions.problem:
Alice designs a new authentication scheme. Let $pwd$ be a secure password that only Alice knows, and let $H^{k}$ be the result of repeatedly applying $H$, a cryptographically secure hash function, $k$ times ($H^{0}(x) = x$ by definition; e.g. $H^{3}(x) = H(H(H(x)))$). Registration: (1) Alice securely generates a 128-bit salt; (2) Alice sends $H^{1000}(pwd \,\|\, salt)$ to the server; (3) the server stores Alice's username and this hash in a variable $stored$. Login for the $i$-th time ($i$ starts at 1): (1) Alice sends $H^{1000-i}(pwd \,\|\, salt)$ to the server; (2) the server checks whether $H(H^{1000-i}(pwd \,\|\, salt))$ equals $stored$; (3) on success the server updates $stored$ to $H^{1000-i}(pwd \,\|\, salt)$.
\begin{tightitem}
\item[(a)] [2p] Justify whether the server needs to know $pwd$ and $salt$ to complete the login process.
\item[(b)] [2p] Eventually Alice logs in by sending $H^{800}(pwd \,\|\, salt)$. Given only $pwd$, $salt$, and $H^{800}(pwd \,\|\, salt)$, how many calls to $H$ does Alice need for the next login request?
\item[(c)] [3p] Eve is a network attacker observing the communication between Alice and the server. At which login attempts would Eve learn some information about Alice's password $pwd$? Justify.
\item[(d)] [3p] An attacker has compromised the server and can modify the variable $stored$. Justify whether the attacker can log in as Alice without knowing $i$, $pwd$, or $salt$.
\end{tightitem}

solution_steps.step_ref: Step 5 (Impossibility / what the server needs -- part a)
solution_steps.work: The server does NOT need to know either $pwd$ or $salt$: login consists entirely of comparing hash values. The server computes ONE hash of the received token and compares it with $stored$; $pwd$ and $salt$ appear in neither operation. The whole chain was built by Alice at registration.

On the next login, $i$ increases by 1, so the exponent $1000 - i$ decreases by 1: it changes from $800$ to $799$. Alice must therefore compute $H^{799}(pwd \,\|\, salt)$. She cannot get it from the $H^{800}(pwd \,\|\, salt)$ she just sent -- that would require inverting $H$ once, and $H$ is one-way. Starting from $pwd \,\|\, salt$ and applying $H$ repeatedly, she needs \[ 799 \text{ calls to } H. \]

The key insight is the 1000th login: Alice sends $H^{1000-1000}(pwd \,\|\, salt) = H^{0}(pwd \,\|\, salt) = pwd \,\|\, salt$, from which Eve reads the password in plaintext. All other logins reveal nothing about $pwd$: they only expose digests, and because $H$ is one-way Eve cannot reverse the chain to reach the original value (the salt additionally provides brute-force resistance).

Yes, the attacker can log in. The server only checks that $H(\text{received token}) = stored$. The attacker picks ANY value $v$, sets $stored := H(v)$ on the compromised server, and then simply provides $v$ as the login token: the server computes $H(v)$, finds it equal to $stored$, and accepts. No knowledge of $i$, $pwd$, or $salt$ is required.

exam_questions.answer: (a) No -- the server only compares hash values; (b) $799$ calls to $H$; (c) at the 1000th login, where Alice sends $H^{0}(pwd \,\|\, salt) = pwd \,\|\, salt$ in plaintext; (d) yes -- set $stored := H(v)$ for a self-chosen $v$ and log in by sending $v$.

exam_questions.source: Exam HT2019 (dasak19), Part II, Problem 4: Authentication -- Passwords [5 points]
exam_questions.problem: The passworth.com web service provider wants to make sure their users' passwords are protected. They take the following measures: (1) Passwords are hashed, not stored in plain text; the hash function was developed and refined over several years by passworth.com experts and kept secret; a salt has been added (the randomly generated prime number 3,184,497,539). (2) Access rights to the stored hashes are given only to the web server (and 3 fallback servers) and a few system administrators. (3) Strict password guidelines: at least 16 characters, at least 2 numbers, 2 special characters, mixed upper/lower case; users must change passwords regularly (once a month, same as the billing cycle). (4) After 3 incorrect password entries the account is blocked, and the user must call the hotline and say their username to get a new password over the phone (to avoid sending passwords by e-mail). You are hired in passworth.com's security team to evaluate the setup. For EACH measure, state concisely: (1) against what threats it protects, (2) what potential vulnerabilities remain or are introduced, (3) which countermeasures you would choose instead, and (4) which factors you take into account for your choice.

solution_steps.work: This is the design-critique variation: there is nothing to compute, but the answer must be organized measure-by-measure along the four required axes (threats countered, remaining vulnerabilities, better countermeasures, decision factors). Grading gave one point per measure for getting most things right, plus a point for clear, concise explanations throughout.

solution_steps.step_ref: Step 8 (Critique each measure) -- Measure 1 (hashing + secret hash + one global salt)
solution_steps.work: Protects against: reading the passwords when someone gains access to the password file (hashing) and against rainbow tables (salt). Remaining vulnerabilities: there is a SINGLE salt for everyone, so the same password still gives the same hash across users -- the salt fails its real job; and the home-grown secret hash function might itself be vulnerable (keeping the algorithm secret violates \term{Kerckhoffs' principle}: security should rest on the key, not on algorithm secrecy). Instead: use individual per-user salts and a well-studied PUBLIC (ideally slow) hash function/KDF such as bcrypt, scrypt or Argon2.

solution_steps.step_ref: Step 8 (Critique each measure) -- Measure 2 (restricted access rights to the hashes)
solution_steps.work: Protects against: wider access to the password file -- fewer principals can read the digests, shrinking the attack surface for offline attacks. Remaining vulnerabilities: web attacks could still exploit the server's access (e.g. injection or file-read vulnerabilities on the web server reach the hashes), and the fallback servers and administrators enlarge the trusted computing base. Instead: strengthen web security and server configuration (patching, least privilege, hardening), not just file permissions.

solution_steps.step_ref: Step 8 (Critique each measure) -- Measure 3 (strict composition rules + monthly rotation)
solution_steps.work: Protects against: dictionary attacks (the rules avoid common, simple passwords) and long-term compromise of a password (the monthly change limits how long a stolen password stays valid). Remaining vulnerabilities: the onerous requirements push users to write passwords down or pick predictable patterns, and forced monthly rotation typically produces weak, predictable modifications (Password1 \rightarrow Password2). Instead: drop the forced policy and turn it into a recommendation (prefer long passphrases, check against breached-password lists), possibly combined with 2-factor authentication.

solution_steps.step_ref: Step 8 (Critique each measure) -- Measure 4 (lockout after 3 failures + phone reset)
solution_steps.work: Protects against: online brute-force attacks (rate limiting via lockout). Remaining vulnerabilities: an attacker can lock out any user at will (user-targeted denial of service), and the password reset has NO authentication -- anyone can call the hotline, give a username, and receive a new password. Instead: send a reset LINK to the user's registered e-mail (or use 2-factor authentication) instead of handing out passwords over the phone; add backoff/captcha rather than hard lockout.

The factors to take into account when choosing countermeasures: cost versus benefit, the level of security the service actually needs, usability (onerous rules backfire into worse user behavior), and the state of security overall at the company.

exam_questions.answer: Measure-by-measure: hashing + secret hash + single global salt partly protects the file but fails Kerckhoffs' principle and real salting (use per-user salts and a public slow KDF); restricted access shrinks exposure but web attacks still reach the server (harden the server); strict rules and monthly rotation counter dictionary attacks and long-term compromise but push users to write passwords down (make it a recommendation, add 2FA); lockout + phone reset counters online guessing but enables user DoS and unauthenticated resets (use e-mail reset links and 2FA).
